new_statements.quote: [p. 97] If most occurrences of word-final accent are attributed to sentence intonation, what remains should be mostly word stress. The pattern that emerges seems to be the following: in words of the form /CVCV(C)/, stress falls on the second syllable; in all other words, it falls on the first syllable. [...] [p. 102] As for the phonetics of stress, it can be said only that it involves some kind of 'loudness' or 'prominence'; there is no indication of any kind of pitch accent or tonal system. In short, stress seems to be a non-phonemic feature of Mutsun. In words of the form /CVCV(C)/ it occurs on the second syllable, otherwise it occurs on the first. Since it is predictable (non-phonemic), stress need not be written in citing forms.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (360 pp., image-only), rendered PDF pp. 107 and 112 (= dissertation pp. 97 and 102) to PNG and read them directly, alongside the scanned file we hold. Both quoted passages are on the page verbatim: p. 97 sec. 142 'Stress Assignment' — "If most occurrences of word-final accent are attributed to sentence intonation, what remains should be mostly word stress.[fn 52] The pattern that emerges seems to be the following: in words of the form /CVCV(C)/, stress falls on the second syllable; in all other words, it falls on the first syllable."; p. 102 — "As for the phonetics of stress, it can be said only that it involves some kind of 'loudness' or 'prominence'; there is no indication of any k…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable (non-phonemic) and falls on the first syllable of the word, except that disyllabic words of the shape CVCV(C) — which derive from underlying CVCV:(C) whose second (long) vowel is shortened word-finally — are stressed on the second syllable; once such a word carries a vowel-bearing suffix (three or more syllables) stress reverts to the initial syllable (koró 'foot' vs. kórotka 'at the foot'). Spanish loanwords take initial stress regardless of Spanish stress. Sentence-final syllables carry an additional intonational accent, which Okrand separates from word stress. Okrand himself calls the description 'conjectural at best' (p. 96) because Harrington's accent marks are erratic; Warner et al. 2022 (p. xix) judge his conclusions too unsure to encode and possibly typologically unlikely.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Harrington's grave accent and circled acute are interpreted as 'secondary stress' or lesser prominence (p. 95), but no rule for secondary stress is given; in sentence-final position an initially-stressed word may also carry final prominence (e.g. /húttúy/), attributed to intonation.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllabic CVCV(C) words (second-syllable stress, tied to underlying final long vowel); stressed long vowels in non-initial syllables (hewé:pas ~ héwé:pas) treated as Harrington confusing length with stress; imperatives sometimes recorded with final stress; the negative particle /?ekwe/ phrase-finally /ekwé/; irregular plural súltukma 'soldiers' deleting the Spanish-stressed syllable; fn. 57 (p. 103): 'there remain many problems with stress, including counterexamples to the above analysis'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress abstracted from phrase/sentence intonation; the data are J. P. Harrington's field notes (1922-1930) from the last speaker, Ascención Solórsano, largely single words in isolation, which Okrand argues carry a sentence-final intonational accent on the last syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Okrand 1977 describes Mutsun proper (muts1243), the San Juan Bautista Costanoan variety, from J. P. Harrington's 1922-1930 notes with Ascención Solórsano de Cervantes (plus Arroyo de la Cuesta's 1815 materials). Mason 1916 and Arroyo 1861/1862 describe the same mission variety. The scan classification the named source could not be reached is now superseded: Okrand 1977 is openly hosted at eScholarship (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1p59z6kq) and on the CLA Box mirror.

sources.note: Ch. 1 sec. 140-142 (pp. 95-103): based on Harrington's erratic accent marks; stress judged non-phonemic; in words of the shape /CVCV(C)/ (from underlying CVCV:(C) with final-vowel shortening) stress falls on the second syllable, in all other words on the first syllable; sentence-final syllables carry an intonational accent; loanwords from Spanish take initial stress; description called 'conjectural at best'; no pitch accent or tone.

sources.note: Introduction p. xix: 'Although Okrand (1977) attempted a thorough analysis of Mutsun stress, he acknowledges that his conclusions about stress are very unsure.. The patterns Okrand identified may also be typologically unlikely as a stress system [fn. 14: p.c. Michael Hammond]. Therefore, we have decided that stress placement is too unsure to encode in the practical orthography.' Suggests future re-analysis from Harrington's diacritics (p. iii).
